code: console.log(typeof null, typeof undefined, typeof NaN);
explanation: Legacy typeof quirks: null returns "object", undeclared/undefined returns "undefined", NaN has type "number".
IEEE 754 binary floating-point rounding causes 0.1 + 0.2 to evaluate to 0.30000000000000004.
Binary + on objects/arrays converts them to primitive strings via toString() before concatenating.
+ concatenates when an operand is a string; - and * coerce string operands to numbers.
Left-to-right chaining: (3 > 2) is true, then true > 1 converts true to 1 → 1 > 1 is false.
Array.sort() converts numbers to UTF-16 strings lexicographically unless given a comparator.
NaN is never equal to itself under == or ===; Object.is() handles NaN identity accurately.
Falsy values are only false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN; non-empty strings & [] are truthy.
var is function/global-scoped (not block-scoped), so inner var a reassigns outer a.
let is block-scoped, creating a separate variable inside { ... } without mutating the outer binding.
var declarations hoist and initialize to undefined before execution reaches the assignment.

code:
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++)
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
explanation: Single shared var i becomes 3 by the time the asynchronous setTimeout callbacks execute.

code:
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++)
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
explanation: let creates a fresh per-iteration binding captured separately by each callback closure.
Synchronous logs run first, then microtasks (Promise.then), then macrotasks (setTimeout).
Objects are assigned by reference, so p and o point to the exact same object in memory.
Array.map passes (value, index) to parseInt(str, radix) → parseInt(2, 1) and parseInt(3, 2) fail as NaN.
Spreading splits characters into an array, reverses them in-place, and joins them back.
Standalone function calls in non-strict mode bind `this` to globalThis.
Extracting o.f into g loses the receiver object context, leaving `this` undefined (or global).

code:
const o = { n: 'x', f: () => this.n };
console.log(o.f());
explanation: Arrow functions capture `this` lexically from their enclosing scope instead of binding dynamically.
typeof 1 evaluates to "number" (a string), and typeof "number" evaluates to "string".
[] coerces to 0 under == false; === rejects different types; null only loosely equals undefined.
Math.max() identity with 0 args is -Infinity; Math.min() identity with 0 args is Infinity.
parseInt parses hexadecimal on "0x" prefix; unary + on "" coerces to 0.
Post-increment returns 5 (a becomes 6), then pre-increment makes a = 7 → 5 + 7 = 12.
Unary +"2" turns "2" into 2 (1 + 2 = 3), then +"3" coerces 3 + "3" into string "33".
Assigning a smaller value to array.length truncates elements beyond that index.
Wrapper objects created with new Boolean() are objects, and all objects evaluate truthy.
Unary +"a" evaluates to NaN, creating "b" + "a" + "NaN" + "a".
Array.includes uses SameValueZero (matches NaN); indexOf uses strict equality (misses NaN).
Set deduplicates with SameValueZero equality, so number 1 and string "1" stay distinct.
Array(3) creates 3 empty slots that join as empty strings separated by 2 hyphens.
The IIFE returns 0 (falsy), and logical NOT (!) flips it to true.
Default parameters trigger only for undefined arguments, not for null.
JavaScript Date months are zero-indexed (0 = January, 11 = December).
An async function always wraps its return value inside a resolved Promise.
Returning a value from .catch() recovers the chain and resolves into the next .then().
Arrays have typeof "object"; use Array.isArray() to distinguish arrays accurately.
Inner let x shadows outer x throughout the entire block, putting console.log(x) in the TDZ.
delete removes the element (leaving an empty hole) and returns true without updating array.length.
Exceeding MAX_SAFE_INTEGER loses integer precision in IEEE 754 doubles.
Function .name returns inferred binding "f"; .length counts formal parameters (0).
When evaluated as expressions, {} + [] coerces via ToString resulting in "[object Object]".
Array concatenation with "" calls Array.toString(), joining elements with commas.
Global isNaN coerces non-numeric strings to NaN first; Number.isNaN checks strictly without coercion.
Array/String .at(-n) indexes cleanly from the end (-1 = last character/element).
Strings are array-like indexed objects whose enumerable own keys are character indices.
Numeric separators (_) improve readability without affecting runtime numeric values.
Nullish ?? triggers fallback only on null/undefined; logical || triggers on any falsy value like 0.

code:
const { a = 1, b = 2 } = { a: undefined, b: null };
console.log(a, b);
explanation: Destructuring defaults trigger only when property is strictly undefined, preserving null.
Labeled continue skips directly to the next iteration of the outer loop labeled `label`.
Spreading converts the string into characters and filter keeps only each character’s first index.
